title: Document stewardship: Digital files preserve professional duties
desc: Addresses access, secure delivery and inadvertent information while distinguishing broad file ownership from minimum end-product rules.

kps.k: Document stewardship remains a professional duty across paper files, electronic records and online legal services.
kps.d: The cluster concerns who may access representation materials, how lawyers must protect them and what lawyers must transfer when representation ends. ABA Formal Opinion 471 grounds surrender in client protection; Restatement § 46 separately addresses safeguarding, inspection and delivery; the Florida Bar packet applies confidentiality and competence duties to digital handling. These materials advance rule-based guidance, not empirical findings about technology’s effects.

qs.q: As noted above, Model Rule 1.16(d) requires a lawyer to take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client’s interest.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

qs.q: Documents Relating to a Representation  (1) A lawyer must take reasonable steps to safeguard documents in the lawyer's possession relating to the representation of a client or former client.
qs.a: Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers § 46: Documents Relating to a Representation · Regulators & courts · 2000

kps.k: The principal divergence concerns broad file access versus an end-product minimum.
kps.d: ABA Formal Opinion 471 reports that most jurisdictions follow an entire-file approach, subject to exceptions the lawyer must establish, but adopts an end-product minimum under the Model Rules. That minimum includes client-provided materials, completed legal documents, relevant correspondence, evidence and requested opinions, without automatically including internal working materials. Restatement § 46 permits inspection and copying of any representation-related document absent substantial grounds for refusal, while separately requiring delivery of documents reasonably needed. Lawyers must distinguish these standards and check applicable local law rather than treat the ABA minimum as a universal rule.

qs.q: A majority of jurisdictions follow what is referred to as the “entire file” approach.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

qs.q: (2) On request, a lawyer must allow a client or former client to inspect and copy any document possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation, unless substantial grounds exist to refuse.
qs.a: Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers § 46: Documents Relating to a Representation · Regulators & courts · 2000

kps.k: Client protection can override the ordinary exclusion of internal work in unfinished matters.
kps.d: The ABA committee generally excludes drafts, research, personal notes and internal administrative materials, particularly after a matter concludes. It reasons that final documents supersede drafts and that preserving intermediate work can impose burdens disproportionate to its value. But where no final product exists and withholding internal materials would harm the client, the lawyer must release them. An imminent filing deadline illustrates why successor counsel may need the latest draft and supporting research, not merely completed deliverables.

qs.q: 27 Thus, drafts and other documents representing work by a lawyer are often of relatively small value to clients and can be burdensome for a lawyer to preserve, catalogue, and maintain.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

qs.q: 33          In this fact scenario, if the lawyer has materials that are: (1) internal notes and memos that were generated primarily for the lawyer’s own purpose in working on the municipality’s matter, (2) for which no final product has emerged, and (3) the materials should be disclosed to avoid harming the municipality’s interest, then the lawyer must also provide the municipality with these materials.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

kps.k: Possession of opposing-party information does not confer unrestricted permission to review or exploit it.
kps.d: The Florida Bar packet distinguishes a client’s deliberate, unauthorised acquisition of documents from inadvertent disclosure. In its scenario, counsel must explain that retention, review or use requires informing the opposing party and must withdraw if the client refuses consent. The packet invokes Hmielewski against misrepresentation and undisclosed exploitation, while acknowledging that the case did not settle counsel’s initial response. Separately, its metadata guidance tells recipients not to seek information they know or should know was unintended and to notify senders of inadvertent receipt; it excludes discovery documents from that guidance.

qs.q: Therefore, neither Rule 4-4.4(b) nor Opinion 93-3 directly govern the inquiring attorney’s situation.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Finally, the inquiring attorney must inform the client that the materials cannot be retained, reviewed or used without informing the opposing party that the inquiring attorney and client have the documents at issue.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Practical compliance requires records policies, secure handling and suitable delivery arrangements.
kps.d: ABA Formal Opinion 471 treats electronic communications as subject to the same surrender duties as paper and recommends ongoing document sharing and reasonable agreements about file maintenance, format and costs. The Florida packet encourages, but does not mandate, electronic storage; it calls for precautions with third-party conversion and storage, metadata and device disposal. Its Internet-practice guidance also requires lawyers to change delivery methods or decline matters too complex for online handling. These positions permit efficiency gains without relaxing professional duties.

qs.q: The use of the term “paper” in Rule 1.16(d) includes all communications noted above, whether tangible or electronic.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

qs.q: Finally, lawyers must take reasonable precautions to ensure confidentiality of client information, particularly if the lawyer relies on third parties to convert and store paper documents to electronic records.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The guidance leaves important legal entitlements and implementation questions unresolved.
kps.d: ABA Formal Opinion 471 addresses ethical duties, not property rights, and excludes retaining liens because its lawyer has been paid. It does not set initial retention requirements or resolve electronic-to-paper conversion duties and costs; the Model Rules do not directly prescribe a post-representation preservation period. Florida’s advisory opinions are nonbinding and distinguish ethical notice duties from legal questions about return, criminality and privilege waiver. The supplied Restatement text incorporates a § 43(1) exception without explaining it and lacks commentary. These limits caution against treating the materials as exhaustive statements of file rights.

qs.q: The opinion does not address a client’s property rights or other legal rights to these materials.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

qs.q: Whether the lawyer is required to take        additional steps, such as returning the original document, is a matter of law        beyond the scope of these rules, as is the question of whether the privileged status        of a document has been waived.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional bodies support the proposition that moving documents into electronic files or online delivery does not dilute lawyers’ duties of safeguarding, confidentiality, client protection and appropriate transfer. Their common reasoning is rule-based: existing professional obligations attach to representation information regardless of medium, while practical compliance requires reasonable security and context-sensitive handling. Material variation concerns the scope and source of those duties. Restatement § 46 provides broad inspection and copying rights while making delivery depend on reasonable client need and specified exceptions. ABA Formal Opinion 471 instead defines a Model Rules ethical minimum centred on end products, but requires internal materials where withholding them would harm an unfinished matter. The Florida Bar guidance develops the digital dimension through storage, metadata, device disposal, third-party services, online practice and improperly obtained opposing-party information. These sources also differ in authority and limits: the Restatement text is black-letter but incomplete here, the ABA opinion does not decide property rights, and the Florida opinions are nonbinding and leave some legal questions unresolved. Those qualifications narrow application rather than undermine the principal proposition; this curated set should not be read as representing every regulator, court or professional body.

qs.q: The use of the term “paper” in Rule 1.16(d) includes all communications noted above, whether tangible or electronic.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

qs.q: A lawyer must ensure confidentiality by taking reasonable steps to protect all confidential information under the lawyer’s control.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundation supports the cluster’s principal proposition by establishing that document stewardship entails continuing duties to safeguard representation materials, permit client access and provide timely delivery. Although § 46 does not expressly discuss digital files, its technology-neutral duties provide the professional baseline that the cluster applies across paper and electronic records. Material internal variation lies in the scope of the duties: inspection and copying extend broadly to any representation-related document unless substantial grounds justify refusal, whereas delivery is limited to documents the client reasonably needs and is subject to consent, substantial-ground and § 43(1) exceptions. Because the supplied source contains black-letter provisions without explanatory commentary, it supports the governing framework but does not independently develop the cluster’s later digital-handling guidance. This assessment concerns the curated Restatement source and does not imply that it represents every pre-2015 authority.

qs.q: Documents Relating to a Representation  (1) A lawyer must take reasonable steps to safeguard documents in the lawyer's possession relating to the representation of a client or former client.
qs.a: Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers § 46: Documents Relating to a Representation · Regulators & courts · 2000

qs.q: (3) Unless a client or former client consents to nondelivery or substantial grounds exist for refusing to make delivery, a lawyer must deliver to the client or former client, at an appropriate time and in any event promptly after the representation ends, such originals and copies of other documents possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation as the client or former client reasonably needs.
qs.a: Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers § 46: Documents Relating to a Representation · Regulators & courts · 2000

elens.an: The 2015 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that professional document-stewardship duties continue across paper and electronic files. It expressly treats electronic communications as falling within Rule 1.16(d), grounds surrender in protecting the client’s interests, and requires internal working materials where an unfinished matter would otherwise be harmed. Its internal qualifications concern the duty’s scope rather than its existence: it adopts an end-product minimum rather than universal entire-file access, generally excludes drafts and internal materials in completed matters, recognises that jurisdictions may impose broader requirements, and leaves property rights, initial retention obligations, preservation periods, conversion duties and costs unresolved. Because this time-period facet contains one curated source, the analysis establishes that source’s alignment but does not indicate how prevalent the position was during 2015–2022.

qs.q: The use of the term “paper” in Rule 1.16(d) includes all communications noted above, whether tangible or electronic.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled · Regulators & courts · 2015

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that document-stewardship duties persist across paper files, electronic records and online legal services. Its central reasoning is continuity rather than technological exceptionalism: confidentiality and competence require reasonable safeguards for electronically stored information, metadata, storage devices and third-party services, while ordinary professional-conduct rules continue to govern Internet delivery. It also supports the proposition that possession or technical access does not create unrestricted authority to inspect or exploit information. Material internal variation concerns implementation and scope, not the core duty: electronic storage is encouraged for efficiency but is not mandatory; online delivery is permissible only for suitable matters; and the packet’s nonbinding ethical guidance leaves some legal questions—such as return obligations, criminality and privilege waiver—unresolved. Because this facet contains one curated source, the finding characterises that source rather than the prevalence of this view among regulators or practitioners.

qs.q: A lawyer must ensure confidentiality by taking reasonable steps to protect all confidential information under the lawyer’s control.

qs.q: All rules of professional conduct apply, including competence, communication, conflicts of interest, and confidentiality.
